hero.title: Le Chatelier's Principle — Why Equilibrium Always Fights Back
hero.hook: Why does a fizzy drink go flat faster on a hot day? The answer is one of the most powerful ideas in Chemistry — and it shows up in your board exam every single year.

hook_section.scenario: You open two identical cans of cola. One is ice-cold, one is warm from your bag. The warm one fizzes violently and goes flat in minutes. The cold one stays bubbly for much longer. Why? Both cans had the same amount of CO₂ under the same pressure. What is temperature doing to those bubbles?
hook_section.bridge: This isn't just a fizzy drink puzzle. The same principle explains why car engines knock, why fertiliser factories use specific pressures, and why our blood carries oxygen the way it does.
hook_section.punchline: It all comes down to one rule: a system at equilibrium will always resist change.

concept_section.analogy: Imagine a tug-of-war match where both teams are perfectly balanced — nobody moves. That's chemical equilibrium. Now push one team forward. What do they do? They pull harder to get back to balance. Le Chatelier's Principle is exactly that push-and-pull.
concept_section.principle: Le Chatelier's Principle: "If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, temperature, or pressure, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to reduce the effect of that change."
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each disturbance to see what the system does 👇

reveals.question: 🧪 What if I add more reactant?
reveals.answer: Equilibrium shifts forward (right) — the system tries to consume the extra reactant by making more product.

reveals.question: 🌡️ What if I increase temperature?
reveals.answer: If the forward reaction is exothermic (gives off heat), increasing temperature shifts equilibrium backward — the system absorbs the extra heat. If the forward reaction is endothermic, it shifts forward.

reveals.question: ⬆️ What if I increase pressure?
reveals.answer: Equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas — fewer molecules means less pressure, reducing the disturbance.

reveals.question: 🔩 What if I add a catalyst?
reveals.answer: No shift in equilibrium position. A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally — it helps you reach equilibrium faster but doesn't change where the balance point is.

points: Increasing pressure → shift toward side with fewer moles of gas
Catalyst → reaches equilibrium faster, does NOT shift the position
Haber Process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃): high pressure → more NH₃; but high temperature reduces yield (exothermic reaction) — so 450°C compromise is used

exam_questions.question: Explain the effect of increasing pressure on the Haber Process

quiz.q: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic), what happens when pressure is increased?
opts: Equilibrium shifts backward — more N₂ and H₂
Equilibrium shifts forward — more NH₃ produced
No change — pressure does not affect gas equilibria
quiz.exp: Left side has 4 mol gas (1+3), right side has 2 mol. Higher pressure favours fewer moles, so shifts forward, giving more NH₃.

quiz.q: A catalyst is added to a system at equilibrium. What changes?
opts: Equilibrium is reached faster but position does not change
quiz.exp: A catalyst lowers activation energy for BOTH directions equally. It speeds up reaching equilibrium but cannot change where the balance point lies.

quiz.q: For an endothermic reaction at equilibrium, increasing temperature will:
quiz.exp: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat. Increasing temperature is like adding heat — the system absorbs it by shifting forward.

quiz.q: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq). Why does removing the bottle cap make the drink go flat?
opts: Pressure decreases — equilibrium shifts to produce more CO₂ gas
quiz.exp: CO₂ was dissolved under high pressure (sealed bottle). Opening reduces pressure, so the system shifts to relieve pressure by releasing CO₂ as gas.

flipcards.front: What does Le Chatelier's Principle state?
flipcards.back: A system at equilibrium shifts to reduce any applied disturbance

flipcards.front: Effect of catalyst on equilibrium position?
flipcards.back: NO change in position — only speeds up reaching equilibrium

flipcards.front: In Haber Process, why use 450°C not higher?
flipcards.back: Reaction is exothermic — high temp reduces NH₃ yield; 450°C is a rate-yield compromise
The side with FEWER moles of gas
Forward (right) — to consume the extra reactant

flipcards.front: Why does fizzy drink go flat faster when warm?
flipcards.back: Higher temp favours endothermic reverse reaction — CO₂ escapes from solution
